abstract: Pitch provides a powerful example of perceptual invariance, enabling us to recognize the same melody across different instruments. The fundamental frequency (F0) at which a pitch is heard can be derived from either the harmonic spacing of frequency components (spectral cues), the waveform periodicity (temporal cues), or both. It is unclear whether population codes for F0 in auditory cortex are invariant across these acoustic cue classes. We addressed this question by training a linear decoder to predict F0 from the spiking responses of 1085 neurons in ferret primary auditory cortex to 10 sound types varying in their spectral and temporal composition. F0 could be decoded accurately when trained and tested on any individual sound type. However, decoding performance generalised well across sounds only if they contained the same class of pitch cue, and poorly between complex sounds and pure tones. Onset and offset responses carried different information about the F0 of complex sounds. Finally, approximately 20 neurons were sufficient to decode F0, but F0 information was widely distributed across the neural population. These findings show that F0 is represented in primary auditory cortex in cue-dependent, temporally multiplexed subspaces, with sparse pitch representations embedded in a distributed, robust population code.
